newsitem.title: UK: Author Enid Blyton comes in from literary cold.
newsitem.headline: Author Enid Blyton comes in from literary cold.

text.p: "I wish Enid Blyton were still alive," nine-year-old Tom said wistfully. "I've read nearly all her books and soon there won't be any more left to read."

Blyton's publishers must share that desire, for in the centenary year of her birth sales of her 700 children's stories are soaring worldwide after weathering a storm of political correctness that saw her books banned from libraries and branded racist and sexist.
The centenary birthday was marked on Monday with the unveiling of a commemorative plaque on the wall of the house in Surrey, south of London, where she wrote her first book.
And in a sure sign of literary rehabilitation, over the weekend the Edinburgh Book Festival dedicated a day to the creator of Noddy, the Famous Five and the Secret Seven.
Anna, 12, clutched a battered Secret Seven book treasured by her mother some 30 years ago. Toddlers sported Noddy t-shirts and shiny new plastic editions of his adventures in Toyland.

"There has been considerable growth in sales in the last two years although the Famous Five and the Secret Seven have never gone out of print," said Mary Tapissier, managing director of Hodder Children's Books.

"I don't think there is anyone to touch her in the influence she has on getting kids to read. I think it was a great shame that she was vilified in the 1970s but the message has got home and her books are now regarded as classics," she said.
Blyton, who could turn out a book in five days, died in 1968 and her estate is now a multi-million pound industry owned by children's theme park giant Trocadero Plc.
Her stories have sold more than 200 million copies in more than 40 languages and video sales and merchandising bring in millions of pounds a year.
But 20 years ago it was a different tale. A Blyton backlash headed by teachers and librarians attacked her books for their naughty black golliwogs, rigid gender roles and cosy middle-class values.

Blyton's books were withdrawn from Britain's public libraries and banned from the classroom and the author herself was labelled a hypocrite and an "emotional cripple" by her younger daughter who claimed she neglected her family in favour of her writing.

It is not a view shared by her eldest daughter Gillian Baverstock, who told an audience at the festival how she would rush home from school to pore over her mother's latest adenture as it spilled off the typewriter.
"The story came out complete from her imagination. She didn't have to think about anything in terms of planning or plot," said Baverstock.
"'The Naughtiest Girl in the School' was my favourite story. I wanted to go to a school like that but my mother had to tell me it didn't exist," she recalled.
Noddy, Big Ears and Mr Plod are now headed for a cartoon series in the United States and Canada although the politically incorrect golliwogs, long turned into goblins, will not be accompanying them.
David Rudd, a lecturer and Blyton researcher at Britain's Bolton Institute says literary critics are now being forced to re-appraise her.

"Blyton has been criticised as not worth reading and for being a literary persona non grata. But academics are now trying to get to grips with the paradox that she is still so popular," he told a recent conference.
"She is back out of the cold although quite frankly she never went away. The criticism of her has always been levelled by adults rather than children," Rudd said.
